vocab.q: This trend is likely to ___ in the coming years.

passage: Vertical farming, the practice of growing crops in stacked layers inside controlled indoor environments, has attracted considerable attention over the past decade. Proponents argue that it could ease pressure on agricultural land, which is increasingly scarce as cities expand. Because plants are grown under LED lighting and their nutrients are delivered through water rather than soil, vertical farms can operate all year round, regardless of the weather outside. Some facilities claim to use up to 95 percent less water than conventional fields.

However, the technology is not without its critics. The most frequently cited drawback is energy consumption. Replacing sunlight with artificial light requires vast amounts of electricity, and unless this electricity comes from renewable sources, the environmental benefits may be largely cancelled out. Moreover, the high cost of construction means that most vertical farms have so far focused on leafy greens and herbs, which grow quickly and sell at relatively high prices. Staple crops such as wheat and rice, which feed most of the world's population, remain economically unviable to grow in this way.

Several high-profile companies in the sector have filed for bankruptcy in recent years, prompting some analysts to question whether the industry was overhyped. Others, though, maintain that these failures reflect poor business planning rather than a flaw in the concept itself. They point out that as LED efficiency improves and renewable energy becomes cheaper, the economics of indoor farming could shift considerably. Whether vertical farming becomes a mainstream solution or remains a niche one is likely to depend less on agricultural science than on the price of energy.
